qs.q: A patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency develops panacinar emphysema. Which anatomical lung distribution is most classically expected?
qs.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leads to panacinar emphysema affecting the entire acinus, with a distinct lower lobe predominance. Over eighty percent of patients with severe deficiency develop symptomatic emphysema.

es.q: A 60-year-old male presents with severe dyspnea and a known diagnosis of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Based on this information, identify the most likely type of emphysema and describe its characteristic lung distribution.
es.m: The most likely type of emphysema associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is panacinar emphysema. This subtype primarily affects the lower lobes of the lungs.

es.q: A 60-year-old patient with a known history of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency develops emphysema. Describe the expected pathological subtype of emphysema, its typical location within the lungs, and contrast it with the most common subtype associated with cigarette smoking.
es.m: In a patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, the expected pathological subtype of emphysema is **panacinar emphysema** (1 mark). This subtype primarily affects the **lower lobes** of the lungs (1 mark). In contrast, the most common subtype associated with cigarette smoking is **centriacinar emphysema** (1 mark). Centriacinar emphysema predominantly affects the respiratory bronchioles and adjacent alveoli in the **upper lobes** of the lungs (1 mark), while panacinar emphysema involves uniform enlargement of the acinus from the respiratory bronchiole to the terminal alveoli (1 mark).
es.s: Respiratory System Pathology 1A — Practice Questions — Essay Questions

faq.a: A1AT reaches the lower lobes in lower concentrations, so unchecked neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar walls there.
faq.q: Why does A1AT deficiency cause lower‑lobe emphysema?

faq.a: During acute inflammation levels rise; a normal level then does not exclude deficiency – phenotype/genotype is needed.
faq.q: Can a patient with normal A1AT level still have the disease?

faq.a: It replaces the defective hepatocytes, stopping liver disease, but does not correct the lung problem.

exam: A 35‑year‑old non‑smoker presents with dyspnoea and panacinar emphysema on CT – what is the next diagnostic step? — Order serum A1AT level and phenotype to confirm deficiency.
How does smoking modify the clinical course of A1AT deficiency? — It accelerates emphysema, shifts pattern to centrilobular, and increases mortality; cessation is critical.

A patient with known PiZZ genotype develops jaundice; what investigations are indicated? — Liver function tests, abdominal ultrasound/FibroScan, and hepatitis serology to assess liver injury and rule out co‑infection.
Why is A1AT augmentation not always the first choice in low‑resource settings? — High cost and limited availability; focus on smoking cessation, vaccinations, and bronchodilators.
Differentiate between COPD due to smoking and A1AT deficiency on imaging. — Smoking COPD shows upper‑lobe centrilobular emphysema; A1AT deficiency shows lower‑lobe panacinar pattern.
What red‑flag symptom in an A1AT‑deficient patient warrants urgent admission? — Acute COPD exacerbation with hypoxaemia or new‑onset hepatic encephalopathy.
Explain why a normal A1AT level during infection can be misleading. — Acute‑phase reactants raise A1AT, masking deficiency; repeat testing after recovery.
What is the role of family screening and how should it be performed? — Test first‑degree relatives with serum A1AT level and phenotype; early detection allows preventive measures.
ai.title: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A genetic disorder causing low A1AT levels, leading to early panacinar emphysema and liver disease. Diagnosis relies on serum A1AT, phenotype and genotype, with severity staged by lung function and liver fibrosis.

b: Serum A1AT < 80 mg/dL (adult reference 100‑220 mg/dL) suggests deficiency
Phenotype PiZZ is the most severe; PiMZ is intermediate
sections.p: Alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency (A1ATD) is an autosomal recessive disorder of the SERPINA1 gene causing reduced circulating A1AT, a protease inhibitor that protects lung tissue and hepatocytes.

t.b: Is the protein deficient? – Low level confirms deficiency; normal level rules it out
Which allele is present? – PiZZ = severe, PiMZ = mild, PiSS = rare
Confirms specific mutations – useful for family screening
Is there obstructive disease? – Reduced FEV1/FVC with reduced DLCO indicates emphysema
Is there liver fibrosis? – Increased stiffness suggests progressive liver disease

b: Pulmonary: GOLD stages based on post‑bronchodilator FEV1
Hepatic: METAVIR or FibroScan score; cirrhosis = advanced
sections.p: Severity is staged separately for lung and liver involvement.

b: SERPINA1 PiZZ mutation – severe deficiency
PiMZ – intermediate, often unmasked by smoking or infections
Rare null alleles – virtually no A1AT
sections.p: The primary cause is homozygous PiZZ mutation; heterozygous or other rare alleles give milder disease.

b: Dyspnoea on exertion before age 40, especially in non‑smokers
Chronic cough, wheeze, barrel chest
Hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites in advanced liver disease
sections.p: Patients may present with early‑onset panacinar emphysema (often in the lower lobes) or with liver disease ranging from elevated transaminases to cirrhosis.
Investigations focus on confirming deficiency and assessing organ damage.

t.b: Is the protein low? – Confirms deficiency; if unavailable, use liver function tests as indirect clue
Which allele? – Determines severity; if unavailable, genotype PCR is next step
Obstructive pattern? – Shows emphysema severity; if spirometer unavailable, peak flow trends can be used
What is the pattern of emphysema? – Lower‑lobe predominant panacinar emphysema is classic
Is the liver injured? – Elevated ALT/AST, GGT suggest hepatic involvement
Is there fibrosis? – Stiffness > 7 kPa indicates significant fibrosis

b: Acute exacerbation of COPD requiring hospitalisation
Rapidly progressive liver failure or variceal bleeding
Bronchiectasis with recurrent infections
Pulmonary hypertension secondary to emphysema
sections.p: Complications arise from progressive lung and liver damage and from infections that accelerate decline.

b: Smoking cessation – eliminates major trigger
A1AT augmentation (IV purified A1AT) – slows lung decline; not always available in low‑resource settings
Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B) – prevent infections
Bronchodilators (LABA/LAMA) for symptomatic COPD – improve airflow
Liver surveillance: ultrasound every 6 months, refer for transplant if cirrhosis
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., high‑dose acetaminophen) – protect liver
sections.p: Management combines avoidance of lung injury, augmentation therapy where available, and treatment of liver disease.

b: Spirometry every 12 months; earlier if symptoms worsen
Liver ultrasound or FibroScan annually
Family screening of first‑degree relatives
Education on environmental exposures (dust, biomass smoke)
sections.p: Regular monitoring of lung function and liver status is essential.

b: Smoking‑related COPD – usually centrilobular, upper‑lobe dominant
Alpha‑1 antichymotrypsin deficiency – rare, similar protease inhibitor defect
Chronic hepatitis B/C – liver disease without emphysema
sections.p: Conditions that cause early emphysema or liver disease may be mistaken for A1ATD.

b: Acute phase reaction raises A1AT level, giving false‑normal result – repeat when patient is stable
Heterozygous PiMZ may have borderline A1AT; clinical context decides
Chest X‑ray may appear normal early; CT is more sensitive
sections.p: Certain factors can mask the true severity of A1ATD.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness with cyanosis
